02 — The process

One sealed chamber, six disciplined steps

The S-1688 is a batch chamber, not a conveyor: one stencil per cycle, washed and dried in the same sealed volume.

01

Load and centre

The operator opens the inner door with the safety button, slides the stencil onto the chute rollers and centres it in the fixture.

02

Seal the double door

Inner cleaning door first, then the outer safety door. The interlock lamp only lights when both are closed.

03

Rotary double-side wash · 2–4 min

The pneumatic diaphragm pump drives solvent through asymmetric rotating spray arms that jet both faces of the stencil at an adjustable 0.2–0.3 MPa.

04

High-pressure air dry · 2–5 min

The same rotary arms switch to high-pressure air and blow the stencil dry in the chamber.

05

Three-stage solvent recycling

Returning solvent passes 10 µm, 5 µm and 1 µm stages before it re-enters the pump.

06

Counted, logged, serviced on time

Every cycle increments the pneumatic counter (0–999,999). At 1,500 counted cycles the manual schedules a filter-element change.

Cycle times, pressures, filtration stages and counter interval quoted from the S-1688 user manual.

Why the build is pneumatic and stainless

SUS304 body and piping

Chamber, liquid pipes and corner valves are stainless steel — no plastic wetted parts.

No electricity in the wash room

Every actuator is pneumatic logic: pump, timers, counter, interlocks.

Double-door interlocked chamber

Inner cleaning door plus outer safety door with an interlock: the machine will not start open and stops when opened.

Modular controller, quick-plug service

Pneumatic timer and control modules pull out on quick connectors.

Automatic fill and drain

A ball-valve manifold and the diaphragm pump add and discharge solvent through hoses.

Named-brand pneumatics

Ingersoll Rand diaphragm pump; Festo or Hengstler pneumatic timer; SMC or Koganei switches and indicators, by production batch.

Controls an operator can trust with gloves on

Pneumatic timer, 10–999 s per stage

Wash and dry times are set on protected dials with lock caps.

Cycle counter to 999,999

Each cleaned stencil increments the counter. The manual schedules the filter-element change at 1,500 cycles.

Lockable pressure regulator

Source pressure held near 0.4 MPa, cleaning pressure adjusted to 0.2–0.3 MPa and locked.

Interlock and emergency stop

Safety-door lamp, inner-door safety button and a mushroom emergency stop.

06 — Installation

What your floor needs before the crate opens

The manual's installation chapter is short because the machine asks for little: air, exhaust, ground and space.

STEP 1

Site and environment

Dry, ventilated, clean and flat floor away from fire and heat sources. Keep at least 3 m distance from electrical equipment.

STEP 2

Compressed air

0.4–0.6 MPa on a Φ12 mm line with a quick joint. Below 0.4 MPa the machine will not start; above 0.6 MPa risks the pneumatic system.

STEP 3

Exhaust

Top Φ125 mm outlet ducted independently to outside. The manual forbids connecting it to any heat-source equipment.

STEP 4

Grounding

Connect the ground wire on its own earth point, never shared with other equipment.

STEP 5

Service clearance

At least 1 m around the cabinet for filter changes, tank cleaning and pneumatic-module service.

STEP 6

No electrical work at all

There is no power connection to plan. Commissioning is: air pressure check, solvent fill above the M mark, ball valves A and D open with B and C closed, then one button.

ARTICLE 01Your printer is not the problem — your stencil is

Print defects that survive inspection usually started as residue in an aperture.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Stand at your screen printer for one shift and count the pauses. The operator wipes the underside, re-checks the deposit, adjusts something nobody can name. The machine is fine. The stencil is the variable — and nobody measures it.

Here is what the residue actually does. Dried paste narrows an aperture by a few microns on one side of the frame and more on the other. The deposit volume drops, the release gets stochastic, and the defect walks out of printing as a "random" bridging or shortage that inspection catches — or does not. By the time anyone blames the printer, the stencil has already printed two hundred boards of quiet variance.

You can audit this today without buying anything. Three points, one sheet of paper. First: hold a "clean" stencil against a light table after thirty prints — count the apertures that glow unevenly. Second: swipe a lint-free wipe across one face and look at what came off. Third: ask what the last cleaning actually was — a machine cycle with a timer, or a wipe with a spray bottle and optimism. If the third answer makes anyone laugh, the first two answers already made them cry.

The method that fixes it is boring on purpose: a closed chamber that runs the same recipe every time. The S-1688 sprays both faces with rotary arms at a pressure you set and lock — 0.2–0.3 MPa, enough to dissolve paste and red glue, gentle enough that mesh tension stays where the printer needs it. The solvent recycles through three filtration stages, and a pneumatic counter logs every cycle so filter changes happen on evidence, not on memory.

Keep the audit on the wall and repeat it every quarter — and after every paste, flux or squeegee change. The first audit finds the residue; the second finds the process change that reintroduced it. Factories that re-audit catch escapes while they are still a trend line, not a recall.

Want the three-point audit run for you? Send a photo of a "clean" stencil from your line to info@smthelp.com or on WhatsApp at +86 13602562576. We will light-table it, photograph what comes off on a wipe, and tell you honestly whether your screens need this machine at all.

ARTICLE 02Nine minutes per stencil: the rhythm that keeps print quality honest

Wash 2–4, rinse 2–4, dry 2–5: the manual's own cycle maths.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Print quality is a rhythm, not a heroics performance. The stencil that goes back on the printer half-clean, damp, or "good enough for now" resets your defect rate for the next hundred boards. So the honest question is not whether to clean — it is whether cleaning has a rhythm you can schedule.

Our S-1688 user manual publishes the rhythm as plain numbers: wash two to four minutes, rinse two to four, dry two to five, each stage set on a pneumatic timer between 10 and 999 seconds. A standard stencil — paste plus a little flux bleed — lands near three minutes per stage. Add about a minute to load, seal the double door and unload, and one clean, dry, counted stencil leaves the chamber in nine minutes.

Why does the fixed number matter more than the fast one? Because variance is what kills printing. A bench wipe takes two minutes when the operator is relaxed and twenty when they are not, and the board cannot tell which one it got. A timer cannot have a bad shift. Set it once, lock the cap, and every stencil of the day receives the same recipe — the same pressure, the same dwell, the same dry.

Nine minutes per stencil is also a scheduling gift. Clean between products, not between disasters: when the job changes, the outgoing stencil goes in the chamber while the setup for the next job is being fetched. The machine runs on plant air and needs no one watching it; the counter tallies the cycle so your maintenance clock keeps itself honest.

If your current rhythm is "whenever someone remembers," start measuring for one week — cleanings per stencil, minutes per cleaning, defects per roll. The numbers will make the decision for you, and they will make it in the direction of the timer.

Tell us your stencil count per shift and we will send back the cycle plan — chamber time, filter life at your volume, and the air demand your compressor needs to see. info@smthelp.com, or WhatsApp +86 13602562576.

ARTICLE 03Manual stencil scrubbing: the cost that never appears on the floor plan

Wages, variance, solvent evaporation and spent tension — four lines that price the bench.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Every factory that cleans stencils by hand eventually does the same math, badly. Somebody counts the wipe-and-spray minutes and decides the bench is "basically free." That count is missing three lines — and the missing lines are where the money went.

Line one is the obvious one: the wages. Fifteen minutes a stencil, six stencils a day, at a loaded hourly rate, every working day of the year. Run it before you decide it is small. Line two is the variance: hand cleaning removes what the operator saw, which is why the same product prints differently after the 11 a.m. wipe than after the 4 p.m. one. Variance does not show up as a cost line; it shows up as rework nobody files under "cleaning."

Line three is the mesh. Brush pressure and open solvent spend stencil tension the way highway spending burns fuel — invisibly, continuously, until one day the frame is scrap and the replacement invoice lands on a desk that never budgeted for it. Tension is a consumable; scrubbing is the rate you consume it at.

Line four is the room. Open-can solvent evaporates into your air: the fire officer's paperwork, the ventilation survey, the waste manifest, the operator who prefers not to lean over the bench. None of it appears on the cleaning budget, all of it appears somewhere else.

The replacement is not exotic. A sealed pneumatic chamber takes the same fifteen minutes of attention and turns them into one button: load, close two doors, start. Wash and dry run behind steel on a locked timer, the solvent recycles through three filter stages instead of evaporating into the room, and the counter records every cycle so the only human decision left is when to change the elements — which the machine tells you at 1,500.

Price your bench on all four lines for one month, then compare it against the calculator on this page. The bench almost never wins twice.

ARTICLE 04Why the stencil cleaning room should run on air, not electricity

Solvent vapour and ignition sources do not belong in the same room.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Think about the two ingredients of stencil cleaning: a flammable or volatile chemistry, and a machine that has to do work. In most factories the second ingredient is an electric motor with switches, brushes and relays — and the first is sitting in an open tray next to it. Nobody chose that combination; it is just what "cleaning machine" meant.

The S-1688 was built the other way around. Every function — pump, spray rotation, timing, counting, door logic — runs on compressed air at 0.4–0.6 MPa. There is no motor in the chamber zone, no switch to arc, no wiring to fault. The user manual states the reason in one line: no power supply, no fire hazard. Where solvent vapour lives, the machine brings only air.

The safety case does not stop at ignition. The process runs behind a double door with an interlock: the machine will not start open and stops the moment a door is opened mid-cycle. The operator never meets the cleaning fluid — not during the wash, not during the dry. And because the solvent is recycled through a three-stage filter train instead of sitting open, what does not evaporate into the room also does not need to be bought back every week.

There is a quieter benefit too: a pneumatic machine is maintainable by the people who already fix your line. The timer is a dial, the control modules pull out on quick connectors, and the pressure regulator locks. No controller to re-flash, no electrician to schedule, no firmware to fear. The failure modes are mechanical, visible, and the manual already lists them.

None of this means "plug it in and forget it." Solvent handling still demands gloves, glasses and a respirator at the fill and drain steps — the machine protects the cycle; you still protect the person. But it does mean the room where vapour and work meet no longer needs a compromise between them.

If your current cleaner has a power cord and a solvent tray, send us a photo of the setup. We will tell you what the same duty looks like running on air alone.

ARTICLE 05Stencil tension is a consumable — stop scrubbing it away

Brush pressure spends mesh life faster than printing does.

Articles are marketing commentary.

You treat tension like a constant. It is not — it is a budget, and every cleaning either spends a little of it or spends none. The frame is stretched to a precise force so the mesh snaps clean away from paste; scrub that mesh with a brush and solvent and the bond line between foil and frame slowly gives up microns. Nobody notices until the print does.

The symptoms arrive in a predictable order: gasketing leaks paste under the frame, the deposit gets thin near the middle and fat at the edges, and the "random" bridging reports start naming one side of the panel. By then the stencil is past the point where cleaning could have saved it — because the cleaning is what spent it.

So the rule we give customers is simple: the mesh never sees a brush, and the spray never sees more pressure than the job needs. That is exactly what the S-1688 manual encodes. Cleaning pressure is adjustable and typically held at 0.2–0.3 MPa — the manual states the adjustment exists to keep steel-mesh tension stable. The rotary arms spray both faces at equal pressure, so the foil is never pushed toward one side of its own tension.

The other tension-killer is heat and chemistry left sitting. Paste residues are mildly aggressive; left to dry, they attack the aperture walls and the bond line in slow motion. A rinse inside the same sealed cycle, followed by a high-pressure air dry, removes the chemistry before it can spend your budget. Two to four minutes of wash, two to five of dry — the manual's own numbers — and the stencil goes back on the printer with the same force it left with.

Track it like the consumable it is: log tension readings at the same interval you change filters, and the cleaning method you chose will argue for itself. Factories that measure stop scrubbing; factories that scrub keep buying stencils.

Send us your tension spec and mesh type and we will recommend the pressure and chemistry pairing that protects it — info@smthelp.com.

ARTICLE 06Three filters, one solvent bill: how recirculating cleaning pays for itself

10/5/1 µm stages, a 40 L working fill and a counter that schedules the change.

Articles are marketing commentary.

The open-can model of stencil cleaning has a hidden fuel gauge: the solvent level. Every wipe throws away what evaporated, every tray is scrapped with the dirt still in it, and nobody reconciles the drum purchase against the boards printed. Recirculation turns that leak into a closed account — and the account is audited by filters.

Here is the S-1688 ledger, from the manual. A 40-litre working fill (in a 50-litre tank) circulates through three stages: 10 µm takes the coarse debris — dried paste chunks, glue film; 5 µm polishes out the mid-range; 1 µm catches the solder balls and pigment that would otherwise redeposit on a "clean" face. What leaves the circuit is the dirt the filters catch, not the solvent itself. Losses at change-out are measured in litres, not drums.

The consumable discipline is instrumented, which is what makes it survive contact with a busy floor. A pneumatic counter increments with every stencil, and the manual schedules the filter-element change at 1,500 counted cycles. No one decides when the filters are "probably" done; the dial does. Our catalogue puts the money figure next to it: a pair of elements around thirty-five to forty US dollars supporting more than two hundred screens between the documented service intervals — the two numbers from our two documents are both printed here because both are ours.

Recirculation also stabilises quality, which is the part that never makes it into a savings sheet but always shows in the defect chart. A fresh spray of clean solvent dissolves paste; a tired, particulate-loaded one polishes dirt across the mesh. Three stages of filtration mean the nozzle sees the same chemistry on cycle one and cycle nine hundred — the printer cannot tell the difference, which is exactly the point.

Do the audit before you buy anything: pour last week's solvent bills into one column and last week's stencil purchases into another. The second column is usually the one that argues for the machine.

We will model the filter and solvent cost at your stencil volume — send the daily count to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576.

ARTICLE 07One chamber, every screen: paste mesh, red glue stencil, copper mesh

Why the same sealed cycle handles your whole screen park — and when the dual-chamber S-1688B is the better answer.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Ask a print supervisor what the cleaning machine is for and they will say "stencils." Ask their purchasing history and the answer gets wider: the glue screens for SMD adhesive, the copper mesh for RF work, the microporous screens for fine-pitch paste, the squeegees that accumulate paste at the bead line, the fixtures that come back from wave solder with flux boot. One screen type per machine is how factories end up with three machines and still a queue.

The S-1688 manual lists the whole park as its application: stencils, glue screens and copper mesh as primary loads, with wire mesh, microporous mesh, squeegees, fixtures and PCBs named as documented secondary loads. The mechanism is one size fits most — a chute with rollers that centres the screen in the fixture, rotary arms that spray both faces, and a pressure you dial to the job: 0.2–0.3 MPa for a tensioned paste stencil, the upper end for a rugged glue screen, water-based or solvent chemistry chosen per residue family.

There is one design decision the single chamber cannot dodge, and it is chemistry. Red-glue strippers and paste-dissolving solvents do not want to share a tank; lead-free and leaded paste residues argue about the same bath. That is the job of the S-1688B: two independent chambers, two solvent circuits, side by side — paste meshes on the left, glue screens on the right, with zero cross-contamination and double the cycle rate. The same button, the same filtration logic, twice.

The sizing rule we use on audits: if your screen park is one chemistry family and under roughly eight stencils an hour, the single chamber runs it. Two families, or a high-mix shift that never stops printing, the dual chamber pays for the second door before lunch.

Send us the list of what actually gets cleaned in your print room — not what should, what does — and we will tell you one chamber or two, in writing.

ARTICLE 08Five questions to ask before you buy any stencil cleaner

Chamber versus screen size, air demand, exhaust routing, filtration stages and interlocks.

Articles are marketing commentary.

A stencil cleaner is one of the few purchases where the brochure and the manual can be checked against each other in five minutes. Use these five questions on any vendor — including us — and write the answers down. The machine that survives the exercise is the one to buy.

One: does the chamber fit your largest screen, with the door closed? The S-1688 answers with a number from the manual — standard 29-inch stencils and below — and the 2019 deck answers with the chamber geometry, 750 × 750 × 40 mm. If a vendor cannot quote both, they are guessing. Two: what does it actually consume? Air: 0.4–0.6 MPa at 400–600 L/min per circuit. Solvent: a 40-litre working fill, recycled. Electricity: none. Ask for all three; consumption is the spec sheet's shadow.

Three: where does the vapour go? A sealed chamber needs a sealed exhaust path — the S-1688 carries a Φ125 mm top outlet that the manual requires to be ducted independently outside, and explicitly forbids sharing with heat-source equipment like reflow or wave. If the exhaust answer is "the room," the room becomes the filter.

Four: how many filtration stages, and what changes them? One barrel is a strainer; three graded stages — 10, 5 and 1 µm — are a recycling system. Ask what schedules the change: a person's memory, or a cycle counter. The manual's answer for the S-1688 is a counter that reports 1,500 cycles to the filter change.

Five: what stops the machine from hurting someone? Double doors with an interlock that refuses to start open and stops when opened, an emergency stop, a fully closed process so nobody meets the fluid. Then ask the follow-up: what protects the person anyway? Gloves, glasses, respirator at fill and drain — the machine protects the cycle, PPE protects the person, and any vendor who skips the second half has not read their own manual.

Run the five questions against your current setup and the answer is usually not "buy a machine" — it is "name the process." When you are ready to name it with numbers, the calculator above and our quotation desk use the same manual. info@smthelp.com · WhatsApp +86 13602562576.
